standard.title: Create civic arguments
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have created civic descriptions, explanations and arguments at Year 7 level (AC9HC7S05). The gap this descriptor fills is creating civic communication that references evidence — moving from basic descriptions and explanations to arguments that are grounded in evidence and use subject-specific terminology accurately. The command term 'create' encompasses a range of output types — not just written arguments but also descriptions and explanations across different civic contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence — including persuasive content on contemporary civic issues and accurate use of subject-specific legal and civic terminology.

nodes.label: Civic concepts and terminology
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use appropriate civics and citizenship concepts and terms accurately in their descriptions and explanations — including terms such as 'freedoms', 'responsibilities', 'common law', 'statutory law' and 'customary law'.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least three subject-specific civics terms accurately in a short description or explanation of a civic concept.
nodes.typical_width: Demonstrate accurate use of appropriate civics and citizenship terms and concepts — including 'freedoms', 'responsibilities', 'common law', 'statutory law', 'customary law' and other Year 8 civics vocabulary — in descriptions and explanations of political and legal concepts.
wider: Investigate how the same civic concept (e.g. 'rule of law' or 'democratic participation') is defined and used differently in different contexts — academic, legal, journalistic, political — and analyse what precision of terminology matters in each context

Practise writing for different audiences about the same civic concept, adjusting terminology use while maintaining accuracy (e.g. for a Year 8 peer vs for a formal submission vs for a general public audience)
Build a personal civic vocabulary reference — tracking how terms are defined, used in context and applied across different civics topics throughout the year
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate vocabulary is the prerequisite for all subsequent civic argument creation. Arguments that misuse civic terms cannot be evaluated as civic arguments — the evidence cannot be connected to the claim if the claim is not expressed with precision. This foundation underpins all outputs in S05.

response_modes.reason: Accurate term use requires repeated, varied practice before it becomes fluent. This is not a concept students understand once — it needs consolidation across multiple description and explanation tasks before the vocabulary is truly usable.

success_criteria: Can use at least three Year 8 civics terms accurately in a description or explanation
Can distinguish between two related terms (e.g. statutory law vs common law, or civil law vs criminal law) in writing

nodes.label: Evidence-referenced civic descriptions and explanations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create civic descriptions and explanations that reference evidence — connecting claims to sources or examples rather than making unsupported assertions.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a civic description or explanation that references at least one piece of evidence (fact, example or source) to support a key claim.
nodes.typical_width: Create civic descriptions and explanations that use subject-specific knowledge and terminology and that reference evidence — connecting claims to specific examples, case studies, statistics or cited sources — demonstrating that assertions about political and legal systems are grounded rather than opinion-only.
wider: Practise creating descriptions and explanations for different civic audiences — comparing how evidence is referenced differently for a formal report versus a public information piece versus a student essay
Examine how different types of evidence (statistical, anecdotal, expert opinion, legal precedent) function differently in civic descriptions and explanations, and practise using each type
Analyse exemplar civic descriptions and explanations — identifying where evidence is used effectively, where it is missing and what stronger evidence use would look like

response_modes.reason: Evidence-referenced writing is a transferable skill. Widening across different civic topics and different output types — descriptions, explanations, reports — builds the habit of evidence-grounding across contexts, not just in one assessed task.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Evidence-referencing in civic writing is both a discipline-specific skill and a general academic literacy skill. Width across different civic topics and output types builds transferable capability that students will use across their schooling.
success_criteria: Can write a civic description or explanation that includes at least one explicitly referenced piece of evidence
Can explain why the evidence they have chosen supports the claim it is linked to

nodes.label: Persuasive civic arguments with evidence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create civic arguments — including persuasive writing — that use knowledge, concepts and terms accurately and that reference evidence to support the position argued.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a short persuasive civic argument on a contemporary issue that uses at least two civic terms accurately and references at least one piece of evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Create persuasive civic arguments — such as a case for constitutional change or an advertisement promoting participation in Australian democracy — that use civics knowledge, concepts and appropriate terminology accurately, and that reference evidence to support the argument, demonstrating understanding of audience and purpose.
wider: Create civic arguments in multiple formats for the same issue — comparing how a written essay, an oral speech, a social media post and a formal submission each require different approaches to evidence and terminology

Investigate and critique an existing civic argument (e.g. a parliamentary speech, a public advocacy piece) — evaluating the quality of evidence use, accuracy of civic terminology, and persuasive effectiveness

Develop a multi-component civic communication product on a contemporary issue — combining a factual description, an explanatory piece and a persuasive argument to serve different audience needs on the same issue

response_modes.reason: Persuasive civic argument is the integration point for all skills developed in S01–S05: inquiry questions shaped the research, source organisation and perspective analysis informed the evidence, and terminology fluency from earlier nodes provides the language. This is the full descriptor demand — coordinate all components in the argument creation.

success_criteria: Can write a civic argument that takes a clear position, supports it with at least one piece of referenced evidence, and uses civic terminology accurately
Can explain how the evidence chosen supports the argument rather than simply including it as decoration
